To compare designs, we can group their energy costs by where the work occurs. The decomposition below separates computation, memory, interconnect, control, and leakage. Each term must be estimated for the workload and implementation being studied; the historical reference ratios do not supply those totals.
$$
E_{\mathrm{system}} = E_{\mathrm{compute}} + E_{\mathrm{memory}} + E_{\mathrm{interconnect}} + E_{\mathrm{control}} + E_{\mathrm{leakage}}
$${#eq-system-energy-decomposition}

The decomposition in @eq-system-energy-decomposition gives the memory hierarchy an explicit place in the comparison. The *memory wall* described by @WulfMcKee1995HittingMemoryWall concerns the growing importance of memory stalls as processors improve faster than memory latency. Its consequence depends on how often the workload reaches the slower level and how much latency can be hidden. The energy comparison similarly depends on traffic, rather than access cost alone.

Communication among cores and accelerator tiles adds another term. Offered traffic can exceed a network-on-chip link's capacity, causing queueing and backpressure even when the arithmetic units have spare capacity. The physical layout must also provide the wires needed by the chosen topology. Network traffic congestion and physical routing congestion are related implementation concerns, but they are not the same phenomenon.

The proxy-mismatch failure appears directly when comparing total system energy between a balanced baseline design and an unoptimized accelerator candidate (@fig-waterbed-effect). The candidate shrinks compute energy ($E_{\mathrm{compute}}$), yet its added memory accesses and communication overhead swell memory and interconnect energy ($E_{\mathrm{memory}} + E_{\mathrm{interconnect}}$) enough to push the system total above the baseline. Reducing compute energy in isolation can thus increase data movement and interconnect energy, inflating total system energy and causing partial evaluation metrics to rank an inferior design first.

![**Local compute energy reductions can obscure total system energy increases.** A stacked energy breakdown compares a balanced baseline against an illustrative accelerator candidate. While the candidate reduces compute energy ($E_{\mathrm{compute}}$), unoptimized data movement and interconnect traffic swell memory and interconnect energy ($E_{\mathrm{memory}} + E_{\mathrm{interconnect}}$), pushing total system energy ($E_{\mathrm{system}}$) above the baseline and causing partial proxy metrics to rank the inferior design first. Bar heights illustrate structural trade-offs and do not represent measured circuit traces.](images/fig-waterbed-effect){#fig-waterbed-effect width="80%" fig-alt="Bar chart comparing a baseline energy breakdown with an illustrative candidate whose lower compute energy is outweighed by higher memory and interconnect energy."}

In @fig-waterbed-effect, the energy terms omitted by a compute-only score are large enough to reverse the ranking. Early models can include interconnect estimates, but placement and routing determine more specific wire lengths, congestion, and parasitic delays [@KahngEtAl2011VLSIPhysicalDesign]. A search guided by an incomplete score may repeatedly favor the configurations for which that omission is most optimistic. Comparing selected candidates with a more detailed model helps reveal the bias.

The same approach applies to power. Early activity and placement estimates can identify a dense mapping that deserves closer analysis even when average power is acceptable. Learned estimates such as PowerNet's IR-drop prediction [@XieEtAl2020PowerNet] can help screen appropriate designs; their validity depends on the inputs and conditions they cover. Electrical supply analysis and thermal analysis must then address their respective effects. A thermal result cannot establish that a rapid current transient is harmless.


Vector execution illustrates this policy interaction concretely. Adding 512-bit vector units to general-purpose CPU cores raises peak floating-point throughput. However, sustained wide-vector execution can raise power and power-delivery demands enough to force the processor to reduce operating frequency. Peak vector width alone does not determine final application speed; architects must measure active-frequency policies alongside the exact mix of vector and nonvector work on the target processor.

During timing signoff, engineering teams evaluate multiple analysis views that pair operating modes with specific process corners using static timing signoff tools such as Cadence Tempus [@Cadence2021Tempus]. A design can clear one view while failing another. Because physical-design tools rely on heuristic optimization, a single failed closure attempt rarely indicates whether the candidate or a flawed tool setup caused the failure. Comparing constraints, seeds, and repeated outcomes separates true design flaws from tool artifacts.

Design-rule checks (DRCs) introduce further physical constraints. Routing must satisfy restricted design rules, including minimum wire and via spacing [@KahngEtAl2011VLSIPhysicalDesign]. Moving a single macro can spawn numerous violations, and repairing one can alter neighboring routes and expose fresh errors. If an automated flow cannot interpret these markers, it shifts a repetitive cleanup and rerouting burden onto implementation engineers.

Interpreting a later physical failure requires the exact design and assumptions that produced it. The retained RTL, parameters, constraints, and implementation outputs let an architect distinguish a design problem from a mismatched input. Electronic design automation (EDA) tools also consume representations beyond RTL, including Library Exchange Format / Design Exchange Format (LEF/DEF) and Liberty timing files.[^fn-lef-def-c02] The execution mechanics are developed in @sec-architecture-environments-tool-interfaces; here the consequence is that preparing and preserving compatible inputs is part of evaluation work.

[^fn-lef-def-c02]: **LEF/DEF and Liberty**: In place-and-route flows, LEF carries the abstract physical information used to place and connect blocks, while DEF records design-specific physical information, such as placement and routing, even before those steps are complete [@Si2LEFDEF]. Meanwhile, Liberty provides characterized cell models covering timing, power, noise, and related behaviors [@Synopsys2012LibertyFormat]. Physical design relies on these implementation formats to expose details omitted from high-level architectural descriptions.

Multi-fidelity methods pair inexpensive models with selected evaluations that resolve their important omissions [@PeherstorferWillcoxGunzburger2018Multifidelity]. The appropriate check depends on the question: gate-level functional simulation, static timing analysis, and thermal analysis provide different information. Using a more expensive tool helps only if it addresses the uncertainty that could change the decision.

While an inexpensive energy proxy supports early screening, candidate finalists require an accurate power model before binding power or efficiency decisions can be made. A design can lead on advertised peak throughput yet degrade on real application workloads due to memory stalls and runtime overhead. One generation of AMD processors illustrates how wide that gap between an advertised specification and delivered work can open in practice.

::: {.callout-war-story title="A design that won on the spec sheet"}
**The claim.** In the Bulldozer generation (Zambezi, 2011), AMD grouped two integer cores behind a shared front end and floating-point unit while pushing clock frequency hard [@BurgessEtAl2011Bulldozer]. Core counts and frequencies are easy to advertise, so they made compelling marketing points. In sharing those structures, the design team traded per-thread capacity for aggregate throughput.
**The gap.** Those figures did not reflect how real workloads used the machine. The shared structures became bottlenecks when threads competed for them, and the higher frequencies raised power draw. The later FX-9590 part carried a 220\ W thermal design power [@AMDFXQuickReference].
**The lesson.** Shared structures must be evaluated with workloads that expose contention, alongside power and frequency behavior. Core count and clock rate alone cannot settle that comparison. AMD's later Zen design placed renewed emphasis on per-core performance and efficiency [@AMDZen].
:::

Because physical constraints and reliability concerns define a vast search space, no early model eliminates the need for robust physical tools to validate final claims. Architects must understand which lower-cost estimates are safe for broad screening, and which rigorous checks retain the power to overturn candidate rankings.

### Simulation Throughput and Fidelity {#sec-stronger-evaluation-expensive}

Once a model includes the effects needed for a comparison, execution time becomes a constraint of its own. Longer workloads and more candidate configurations compete for compute, tool licenses, and the time needed to interpret results. The question is how much representative behavior the available evaluation budget can cover.

Suppose a detailed simulator sustains ten to one hundred thousand target instructions per host second. These are illustrative rates, not a gem5 benchmark. Simulating one second of a workload that retires one billion instructions in that interval would take $10^9/10^5$ to $10^9/10^4$ host seconds, or approximately `{python} f'{1e9 / 1e5 / 3600:.1f}'` to `{python} f'{1e9 / 1e4 / 3600:.1f}'` hours. Multiplying candidates or workload windows can therefore consume the budget quickly even when preparing each run is easy.

Architectural simulators, compiled RTL simulation, hardware emulators, and FPGA platforms offer different ways to trade setup effort against execution capacity. They also model different things. A fast architectural simulator may simplify timing interactions; Verilator executes an RTL model; FireSim uses FPGA acceleration to run full-system, cycle-exact RTL simulations [@KarandikarEtAl2018FireSim]. Their accuracy must be judged for the behavior each model represents. An RTL model can represent functional details absent from an architectural model while still omitting routed wire delays or thermal behavior. The useful tool is the one whose model and execution capacity answer the study's question at an acceptable total cost.

Sampling can reduce execution cost without simply removing model detail. SimPoint selects representative program regions [@SherwoodEtAl2002SimPoint], while SMARTS uses statistical sampling with error estimates [@WunderlichEtAl2003SMARTS]. Analytical screening, sampled detailed simulation, and full-workload execution can therefore complement one another. A study should state which behavior the sample represents, how initialization and warmup are handled, and which conclusions require additional runs.

The allocation decision has two risks: a cheap estimate may discard a promising candidate or send an unsuitable one into an expensive evaluation. More representative simulation can reduce uncertainty about performance, but it does not establish correctness for every behavior the design permits. That remaining obligation leads to verification.


### Verification Bottlenecks

Verification faces an exponential state-space upper bound, even though careful structuring, abstraction, and advanced verification methods govern practical workload size. Adding a single state-holding flip-flop doubles the number of encoded states, meaning a design with $n$ sequential state elements can technically encode up to $2^n$ states. In practice, the reachable subset is far smaller because it depends on reset sequences and valid transition logic; verification flows therefore avoid blind enumeration of every encoded state.

For a large design, brute-force enumeration is generally impractical. Verification teams instead combine functional coverage targets, SystemVerilog Assertions (SVA), formal checks, constrained-random and directed tests, regressions, and unresolved-defect reviews. Coverage describes the behaviors or requirements that the verification plan intended to exercise; a completed coverage target is not proof that every possible bug is absent. A new architectural organization can require new tests and properties even when much of the implementation is reused.

For these reasons, architectural evaluations must explicitly weigh verification effort alongside the classic pillars of power, performance, and area (PPA). For instance, a highly speculative cache-coherence protocol might demonstrate an impressive simulated throughput gain, yet it remains an unacceptable candidate if checking its labyrinth of transient states and race conditions exceeds the design-program budget.

Simulation and formal methods provide different kinds of assurance. Simulation exercises selected behaviors under supplied stimuli. A completed formal proof establishes a stated property for all behaviors covered by the model and its assumptions, but the solver may not be able to complete that proof. Bounded model checking (BMC) searches behaviors up to a specified depth; finding no counterexample within that bound is generally not an unbounded proof. Combinational equivalence checking asks whether two combinational descriptions compute the same Boolean function. These techniques can complement one another, provided that their scopes and assumptions remain explicit [@Clarke2018ModelChecking].

The semiconductor industry has grappled with this verification pressure for over a quarter of a century. As far back as 2001, the International Technology Roadmap for Semiconductors Design chapter declared verification "a bottleneck that has now reached crisis proportions" [@ITRS2001Design]. Today, the Semiconductor Research Corporation's MAPT roadmap explicitly warns of a widening verification gap looming across future technology transitions [@SemiconductorResearchCorporation2023MAPT]. While this history makes verification an indispensable constraint to check whenever someone proposes generating architectural candidates faster, it does not imply that verification will be the limiting constraint in every design program.

A new candidate may need new verification work before its performance matters. Published RTL-generation benchmarks include failures at parsing, interface compliance, and functional testing [@VerilogEval; @RTLLM; @WangEtAl2025OpenRTLSet]. Those tests do not establish timing closure or system correctness, but they show why a plausible description is only a starting point. The cost and latency of producing and checking a candidate depend on its scope, the reused verification infrastructure, and the required assurance; there is no fixed generation-to-verification ratio across abstraction levels.

Staffing surveys give one view of the work involved. In the 2022 Wilson Research Group study, mean peak staffing for IC and ASIC projects had grown by 146% for verification engineers and 50% for design engineers relative to 2007 (@fig-verification-demand-scissors) [@Foster2022WilsonVerificationStudy]. These are relative changes in surveyed staffing, not measurements of the time needed to verify an additional candidate.


The indexed lines in @fig-verification-demand-scissors show why verification capacity deserves explicit attention in a design plan. They do not identify the cause of the growth or determine the bottleneck in a particular project. The next comparison asks a different question: what do the surveys report about first-silicon outcomes alongside that effort?

In the 2024 survey, verification accounted for an average of 58% of project time, while 14% of projects reported first-silicon success [@Foster2025WilsonVerification2024]. The historical series in @fig-ch07-wilson-verification-scissors places these results beside earlier surveys. The population and designs change between studies, so the trends do not establish that additional verification effort caused worse outcomes or failed to help. They show that substantial effort coexists with persistent implementation and integration failures.

![**Verification effort and first-silicon outcomes measure different aspects of the problem.** (a) Survey trends through 2024 include verification time, staffing ratios, and first-silicon success. (b) Reported respin causes in 2024; respondents could select multiple causes. These population-level trends do not isolate causality within a project [@Foster2022WilsonVerificationStudy; @Foster2025WilsonVerification2024].](images/fig-ch07-wilson-verification-scissors){#fig-ch07-wilson-verification-scissors width="100%" fig-alt="Two-panel survey chart for 2002–2024. Verification time rises overall to 58% and first-silicon success falls overall to 14%, with intermediate fluctuations. The verification-to-design staffing ratio reaches 1.16 in 2024. The second panel shows five reported respin causes, led by logic or functional flaws and analog or mixed-signal issues."}

The reported causes span logic, analog integration, clock-domain crossings, timing, and hardware–firmware behavior (@fig-ch07-wilson-verification-scissors b). Clock-domain crossings, for example, require attention to metastability as well as the logical sequence seen by a testbench.[^fn-metastability-c02] More random stimulus alone may poorly exercise a rare interaction; directed tests, suitable constraints, assertions, and formal analysis can target what is missing. The useful question is which failure mechanisms the current checks can detect.

Escaped defects also differ in how they can be repaired. Some permit a firmware or software workaround; others require revised silicon, and a workaround may sacrifice performance or functionality. Intel's \$475M charge associated with the Pentium floating-point division (FDIV) defect illustrates the potential cost of a shipped hardware error [@Edelman1997PentiumDivision; @Intel1995PentiumCharge]. Spectre and Meltdown illustrate a different problem, in which microarchitectural behavior undermines software's security assumptions [@LippEtAl2018Meltdown; @KocherEtAl2019Spectre]. These cases motivate early detection without establishing one universal cost multiplier for every late defect.


Verification effort belongs in the architectural comparison when alternatives differ in the tests, properties, and integration work they require. Reusing a familiar interface may preserve much of that investment; changing the organization may require new checks. The resulting engineering cost, together with implementation and software work, determines which promising designs a program can afford to develop.

\FloatBarrier

## The Economics of Specialized Silicon {#sec-design-cost-pressure}

```{=latex}
\suppressfloats[t]
```

The implementation and verification work described above consumes a finite development budget. Much of that work is non-recurring engineering (NRE): an investment in the design, software, and qualification that precedes production. Its scale matters both when choosing an architecture and when deciding how many alternatives to develop in detail.

Public estimates illustrate the size of this investment (@fig-design-cost-by-node). The Semiconductor Industry Association reports about \$30M for a 65\ nm design in 2006 and more than \$540M for a 5\ nm design in 2020 [@SemiconductorIndustryAssociation2026ChipDesign]. Arm's 2023 prospectus, citing International Business Strategies (IBS), gives estimates of \$249M at 7\ nm and \$725M at 2\ nm [@ArmHoldings2023Prospectus]. These are contextual estimates, not a price list for all chips at a node. Design size, reuse, software scope, and the accounting boundary matter; the roughly \$300M 7\ nm estimate in the plotted McKinsey series differs from IBS's \$249M, and the sources do not specify identical assumptions. The figure identifies its sources rather than treating the combined values as one measured scaling law.

```{python}
#| label: fig-design-cost-by-node
#| fig-cap: |
#|   **Leading-node design estimates illustrate substantial development investment.** The bars combine
#|   public estimates from SIA, McKinsey, and IBS, with sources identified beside each bar
#|   [@SemiconductorIndustryAssociation2026ChipDesign; @BauerEtAl2020SemiconductorDesignManufacturing; @ArmHoldings2023Prospectus].
#|   Scope and accounting differ across sources; these values are neither universal project prices nor a controlled node-scaling experiment.
#| out-width: "100%"
#| fig-alt: "Horizontal bar chart of selected chip design-cost estimates: 30 million dollars at 65 nanometers, 175 million at 10 nanometers, 300 million at 7 nanometers, 540 million at 5 nanometers, and 725 million at 2 nanometers. Each bar names its source; the estimates have different accounting boundaries."

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from _python.plots import COLORS, apply_style

apply_style()

# Sourced constants: data/datasets/chapter2-leading-node-design-cost.csv
nodes = ["65 nm\n(2006)", "10 nm", "7 nm", "5 nm\n(2020)", "2 nm\n(estimate)"]
costs = [30, 175, 300, 540, 725]
sources = [
    "SIA",
    "McKinsey",
    "McKinsey",
    "SIA & McKinsey",
    "IBS (Arm prospectus)",
]

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.4, 2.9))
positions = range(len(nodes))

ax.barh(
    positions,
    costs,
    height=0.58,
    color=COLORS["note_fill"],
    edgecolor=COLORS["constraints"],
    linewidth=1.4,
    zorder=3,
)

for pos, cost, source in zip(positions, costs, sources):
    ax.text(
        cost + 12,
        pos,
        f"${cost}M",
        va="center",
        ha="left",
        fontsize=7,
        fontweight="bold",
        color=COLORS["constraints_ink"],
        zorder=4,
    )
    ax.text(
        cost + 100,
        pos,
        source,
        va="center",
        ha="left",
        fontsize=6,
        color=COLORS["muted"],
        zorder=4,
    )

ax.set_yticks(list(positions))
ax.set_yticklabels(nodes, fontsize=7, color=COLORS["ink"])
ax.invert_yaxis()
ax.set_xlim(0, 1150)
ax.set_xlabel("Reported cost to design one new chip (US$M)", fontsize=7, color=COLORS["ink"])
ax.tick_params(axis="x", labelsize=6.5)
ax.grid(True, axis="x", color=COLORS["grid"], linewidth=0.45, zorder=0)
for spine in ["top", "right", "left"]:
    ax.spines[spine].set_visible(False)
plt.show()
plt.close(fig)
```

The composition of a design budget helps identify where assistance could matter. In the IBS 2\ nm estimate cited by Arm, software development, verification, and IP qualification together account for 71% of the total [@ArmHoldings2023Prospectus]. This is a cost allocation for that estimate, not the fraction of every project's critical path. It nevertheless shows why faster RTL drafting alone cannot be assumed to remove most development expense.

Production volume determines how that upfront investment contributes to each shipped unit. A simple accounting model makes the relationship explicit:

$$
C_{\mathrm{unit}} = C_{\mathrm{variable}} + \frac{C_{\mathrm{NRE}}}{V},
$$

where $C_{\mathrm{variable}}$ is the average manufacturing, packaging, and test cost per shipped unit, $C_{\mathrm{NRE}}$ is the allocated development investment, and $V$ is shipment volume. The model omits financing, pricing, and time-to-market effects, but exposes the central trade-off. A specialized design may save enough energy or system cost to justify its development. At lower volume, those benefits must carry a larger share of NRE per unit. Specialization does not necessarily imply a small market, and a chiplet reused across products can increase the volume over which its development cost is spread.

For a mobile-XR program, the architectural question is whether the expected efficiency and functionality justify the custom hardware, software, and checking work at its anticipated volume. Reusing IP, retaining programmable execution for changing workloads, or choosing a less aggressive process may improve that balance. Each choice can also affect power, performance, and schedule. The useful comparison includes those consequences rather than assuming either that custom silicon is unaffordable or that specialization always pays.

An evaluation budget is part of the same calculation. Spending more on a simulation or integration test can be worthwhile if it resolves an uncertainty that would otherwise cause expensive redesign. Generating more candidates can also be worthwhile if they offer meaningful alternatives. Their value depends on what the complete study learns for the resources it consumes, which brings the chapter's separate pressures back together.

## Compounding Loop Pressures {#sec-compounding-design-loop-pressure}

The preceding sections examined distinct costs, but a design study encounters them together. A different memory organization may need new compiler support; that software changes traffic, which affects the physical and system comparison. Some candidates can reuse existing checks, while others require new verification work. The effort needed to learn from one alternative therefore depends on more than the cost of proposing it.

This tight coupling matters because optimizing one stage often shifts the bottleneck elsewhere. Generating candidates faster risks flooding the evaluation queue. Speeding up simulation risks churning out more results than reviewers can reconcile. Building a more accurate physical model may reveal that none of the available choices hit the target. Design-space size, evaluation capacity, and decision quality are distinct quantities; increasing the first does not guarantee improvement in the other two.

Rather than hunting for a single universal bottleneck, engineering teams should identify the specific work that throttles progress. Teams can measure the age and size of simulation or verification queues, track the fraction of candidates rejected as illegal, or count repeated tool runs and changing inputs. Reviewers can also monitor where results stall waiting for expert judgment. While broad industry trends provide context, local, concrete measurements are necessary to diagnose the actual constraints of a specific design program.

The MAESTRO anchor in @tbl-design-loop-scale-anchors helps make that diagnosis concrete. Its reported analytical throughput makes a large space affordable to score, so a program using such a model should examine work on either side of the search before paying for a faster optimizer. Upstream, a ranking depends on the workload description: changed layer shapes or batch sizes could make an otherwise accurate analytical comparison irrelevant to the deployment. Downstream, a recommendation about implementation may require checks the analytical tier cannot supply. These are possible bottlenecks for a program using the model, not findings that the cited MAESTRO study had stale workloads or an unvetted queue.

This diagnosis includes wasted work as well as slow work. A simulator run against the wrong workload occupies a slot without resolving the pending question, even if it completes successfully. Correcting the inputs can improve useful throughput without making the simulator itself faster.

This possibility extends the classic *design productivity gap* identified in the 2001 ITRS roadmap [@ITRS2001Design] and reiterated in the Semiconductor Research Corporation (SRC) and Semiconductor Industry Association Decadal Plan [@SRCSIA2021DecadalPlan]. Earlier abstraction shifts made larger designs tractable through RTL synthesis and IP reuse. Where candidate construction becomes cheaper, the corresponding challenge is whether simulation, verification, and review can absorb the additional work.

Not every constraint appears as a queue. A study may be waiting for a missing trace or supplier constraint, or its available organizations may all fail the target. In the latter case, faster evaluation of the same alternatives will not produce a feasible design. The architect may need to reconsider the organization, or the requirements, before scheduling more runs.

When the rate of admitting candidates exceeds the rate at which the required evaluations and reviews complete, unfinished work accumulates. The conceptual example in @fig-scissors-gap illustrates that condition. It is not an inevitable consequence of using a generator: selecting fewer candidates, reusing valid results, or improving evaluation capacity can change the balance.

![**Unchecked candidate generation outpaces physical evaluation and review capacity.** In this conceptual relationship, candidate generation velocity outpaces physical evaluation and expert review throughput as architectural scope expands. Beyond the crossover point, unverified proposals accumulate into a widening *scissors gap* of unresolved candidates that have been generated but never evaluated rigorously enough to accept or reject. Accelerating proposal generation without scaling evaluation capacity expands this unvetted backlog.](images/fig-scissors-gap){#fig-scissors-gap width="80%" fig-alt="Conceptual diverging-line diagram in which tool and reviewer capacity initially exceeds work awaiting evaluation. The straight lines cross as design scope and result volume increase, after which work awaiting evaluation rises faster and creates widening unsettled work."}

The diagram becomes a diagnosis only when a program's own measurements show this imbalance. Cheaper generation can encourage the team to admit more work, but the response is a choice about how to spend the saved effort. A familiar observation from resource economics helps explain why total demand need not fall when one activity becomes cheaper.

::: {.callout-law title="The Jevons Paradox of Automated Generation"}
**The principle.** Greater efficiency can encourage enough additional use to increase total resource consumption. Jevons described this possibility for coal use [@Jevons1865CoalQuestion]. It is a conditional response to lower effective cost, not a law that every efficiency improvement raises total consumption.

**The design implication.** If cheaper RTL generation leads a team to submit more candidates to simulation and implementation checks, demand for compute and EDA licenses can rise. The generation saving remains real; the complete study may nevertheless consume more resources.

**The response.** Choose how many candidates to admit and which evaluations each needs, then measure total effort and useful results. Admission limits and staged screening are possible controls (@sec-law-jevons-paradox in @sec-appendix-b-laws-paradoxes).
:::

## Targeting AI Assistance {#sec-where-ai-assistance-targets-design-pressures}

The diagnosis becomes useful when it changes where the team spends its assistance budget. If a missing executable artifact prevents evaluation from starting, drafting that artifact may advance the study. If hundreds of candidates already await simulation, another generator may add delay, while screening or tool automation may help. The same method can therefore be useful in one program and poorly targeted in another.

```{=latex}
\Needspace{10\baselineskip}
```

::: {.callout-design-principle title="Relieve the True Limiting Constraint"}
**The principle.** Start with the work delaying the design decision. Common causes include missing or stale information, expensive evaluation, missing implementations, too many choices for the budget, and time spent operating tools or interpreting failures. These are useful diagnostic categories, not an exhaustive classification.

**The application.** Assess whether assistance reduces the total effort or delay needed to answer the question. Include preparation and review costs, and preserve the checks that the decision requires. The limiting work may change as the study progresses.
:::

These needs suggest several possible uses of AI, from retrieving design information and screening candidates to drafting testbenches and guiding search. @sec-methods-generation-prediction-optimization develops the method choices. Here the purpose is to connect a possible intervention to the work it could save.

For changing software, an automated regression pipeline can rerun the same benchmark with a new compiler and flag a change in candidate rankings. Assistance might help explain which transformation caused the change or identify an input mismatch. The comparison still needs to distinguish an implementation improvement from a changed task. Some of this work may be served well by conventional automation, without a learned model.

The rows in @tbl-ai-contributions-by-bound pair possible assistance with the engineering work it might reduce and the checks that remain. Keeping these together prevents a faster local task from being mistaken for a completed architectural comparison.

| **Limiting work** | **How AI might help** | **Engineering work it could reduce** | **What still establishes the result** |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Context is scattered or stale | Reconcile workload, interface, tool, and result information; flag missing details or stale assumptions. | Manual search across reports, repositories, traces, and prior studies. | Source provenance, versioning, coverage, and architectural judgment that the information is sufficient. |
| Strong evaluation is scarce | Estimate performance, power, physical risk, or uncertainty before a stronger tool is run. | High-fidelity evaluations spent on candidates unlikely to change design decisions. | Calibration against stronger tools, coverage of the relevant design region, and checks on finalists. |
| A needed artifact is missing | Draft RTL, compiler code, tests, constraints, or candidate organizations. | Repetitive artifact creation and the initial pass through a design choice. | Interface rules, compilation or synthesis, verification, and physical checks appropriate to the artifact. |
| The choice space exceeds the budget | Search mappings, schedules, parameters, or topologies under stated objectives and constraints. | Manual sweeps and repeated selection among large numbers of choices. | A complete objective, legal choices, matched evaluation budgets, and stronger evaluation of the selected result. |
| Tool operation or triage consumes attention | Configure tools, launch runs, classify failures, compare reports, and route uncertain cases. | Repeated tool operation and initial result triage. | Clean tool state, reproducible commands, declared tool results, and expert review where required. |
: **Match assistance to the limiting work and retain the necessary checks.** Each row identifies a possible saving and the evidence needed to use its output in a design decision. {#tbl-ai-contributions-by-bound tbl-colwidths="[22,28,24,26]"}

These roles do not determine the workflow by themselves. In the framing of @sec-moonshot, an AI-assisted workflow might use a generator to draft a test. An AI-driven workflow might use predictions to guide automated search within an established design formulation. An AI-native workflow might combine generation, optimization, and evaluation to develop a different hardware–software organization. Prediction, generation, and optimization can contribute to all three; the distinction is how the design work is organized and which choices it can revisit.

The cost of assistance also belongs in the comparison. A surrogate may require data from expensive evaluations; generated candidates require checking; and tool-using systems consume compute, licenses, and review time. These investments may be worthwhile, but their omission can turn displaced work into an apparent saving.

Evaluation standards must also support rejecting AI assistance entirely. An established deterministic method that already solves the limiting task within budget is a serious alternative. A learned method has a poor case when representative training data are unavailable, an adequate independent check cannot be constructed, or training, inference, tool calls, and added review cost more than the engineering work saved. For the illustrative 4,320-candidate sweep, suppose the analytical tier can score every candidate within budget but cycle simulation and synthesis cannot. Under that assumption, a surrogate trained only to replace the cheap analytical calls may save little; a screening predictor calibrated against the expensive tiers is worth costing instead. The candidate count alone does not establish either conclusion. If the primary obstacle is an infeasible requirement, the appropriate response may be to reformulate the architecture question or decline further search.

```{=latex}
\Needspace{28\baselineskip}
```

::: {.callout-lighthouse title="No single method carries the Lighthouse moonshot"}
**Context.** Lighthouse begins with an XRBench-class mobile workload, a 64-bit RISC-V basis, a 3\ W target, and a 3\ nm-class process. It leaves workload instances, memory organization, compiler support, and implementation choices to be developed into a study. The earlier cache and offload examples show why those choices must be considered together.

**Application.** Suppose tuning the existing cache hierarchy leaves too much off-chip traffic. An AI-native design system could propose a tiled execution organization with explicit local buffers, develop the matching transfer interface and software, and compare it with the original design. Optimization could select capacities and tile sizes within each organization; predictions could help choose which candidates warrant implementation. If evaluation exposes excessive launch overhead, the system could generate a revised buffering or invocation organization and test that alternative. Generation introduces architectural alternatives into the loop, while implementation and feedback determine whether they are useful.

**Outcome.** This is a prospective use of the design system, not a completed Lighthouse experiment. It would need to show both that a candidate meets the agreed requirements and that the workflow improves the investigation at a comparable total cost. Merely connecting a generator to tools, or producing a new design description, establishes neither result.
:::

The resulting test is practical: did the chosen assistance help the team answer its architecture question, with the required checks and an honest account of the work? A useful local tool can pass that test without carrying the complete Lighthouse workflow. A broader design system must demonstrate the additional capability its coordination is intended to provide. The architect remains responsible for interpreting the comparison and deciding what further work or review the result warrants.

\FloatBarrier

## Open Questions

The chapter explains why useful architectural progress can be limited by software, implementation, evaluation, or verification work. It does not establish which limit dominates a particular program, or how much an AI-native workflow can change that balance. The remaining questions concern those limits and the evidence needed to understand them.

- **Where does AI assistance produce sustained gains in real design programs?** The limiting work can move as a project develops, and a saving in one stage can add effort elsewhere. Measurements of complete studies are needed to distinguish shorter turnaround, better designs, and work merely shifted into preparation or review. How consistently can the initial diagnosis predict which intervention will help?

- **How should evaluation budgets adapt when search introduces a new organization?** A predictor or analytical model may be well characterized for the existing design family while saying much less about a generated alternative. Spending too little on the unfamiliar candidate can reject a useful idea; spending too much can exhaust the study. How should a design system allocate evaluations when model reliability changes along with the designs being explored?

- **How does architectural generation change the verification work?** Reusing known interfaces may preserve existing tests and properties, while redesign can create interactions that those checks do not cover. It remains unclear when automated generation reduces total engineering effort and when the required verification grows faster than the implementation saving. Can a design system recognize that difference early enough to guide what it proposes?

- **How much flexibility should hardware retain for software that does not yet exist?** Current workloads reveal the benefit of specialization, but cannot fully establish its lifetime value. Programmability, spare capacity, and alternative data paths provide different forms of adaptability at a present cost in area or energy. How can architects compare those investments when future workload changes are only partly known?

- **How can automated exploration use incomplete descriptions of third-party blocks?** Interface documents, supplied models, and observed behavior may each expose only part of a block's constraints. An exploration system must distinguish tested compatibility from assumptions that remain unresolved. What combination of supplier information and targeted testing is sufficient to compare new compositions without treating missing information as permission?

## Summary

Architectural gains increasingly depend on how microarchitecture, specialization, software, and physical implementation work together. The examples in this chapter make the consequences concrete: a faster arithmetic block can lose to offload overhead, a wider vector grouping can increase spills, and lower compute energy can be outweighed by memory traffic. A useful comparison includes the interactions capable of changing its outcome.

Investigating those alternatives consumes implementation effort, evaluation capacity, and verification work. A large search space does not by itself establish an expensive study, and an expensive study does not by itself establish a need for AI. The opportunity depends on the work that limits progress, the alternatives assistance could make practical, and the total cost of obtaining results that answer the architecture question. AI-native redesign is one possible response when the existing formulation excludes useful organizations; its value remains something to demonstrate.

::: {.callout-takeaways}
- **Follow the costs of a local improvement.** Include data movement, control, software overhead, and physical effects before treating a block-level gain as a system gain.
- **Evaluate hardware with its software.** Compiler mappings, runtime behavior, and workload changes can alter which organization is useful.
- **Choose the boundary that answers the question.** Model the interactions that can change the decision, using appropriate abstractions for each scale.
- **Budget for learning from candidates.** Candidate counts, simulation throughput, verification effort, and development cost describe different constraints. Tests, models, and proofs also establish different things.
- **Target assistance and measure the complete result.** Use the workflow and methods the problem needs, including conventional automation. Count preparation, evaluation, and review as well as the task that became faster.
:::

Once a team identifies the work delaying its next decision, it needs a way to organize the study around it. A simulator result must remain tied to the workload and candidate it evaluated, and a failed check must guide the next design action. @sec-architecture-20-ontology develops that organization through six stages: Formulate, Explore, Implement, Evaluate, Interpret, and Commit. Together they connect the architecture question to candidate development, evaluation, interpretation, and the decision about what to do next.


[^fn-mlir-c02]: **MLIR and Triton**: MLIR provides infrastructure for representing and transforming programs at multiple abstraction levels. Triton is a language and compiler for tensor kernels that uses this infrastructure in its compilation pipeline.

[^fn-eda-constraints-c02]: **EDA constraint formats**: Synopsys Design Constraints (SDC) and Unified Power Format (UPF) describe timing requirements and power intent for electronic design automation (EDA) tools. Implementation and verification tools use those declarations to check the design under the specified conditions.

[^fn-shoreline-bandwidth-c02]: **Shoreline bandwidth density**: The communication bandwidth available per unit of die edge, often expressed per millimeter. In a side-by-side chiplet arrangement, interface placement, connection pitch, and signaling rate constrain the bandwidth that can cross the available edge.

[^fn-dark-silicon-c02]: **Dark silicon**: Silicon that cannot all operate concurrently at full performance within the available power and thermal budget. Power gating, clock gating, and reduced operating rates are among the ways a design manages that limit.

[^fn-rtl-c02]: **register-transfer level (RTL)**: A design abstraction which models a synchronous digital circuit in terms of the flow of digital signals (data) between hardware registers, and the logical operations performed on those signals.

[^fn-rc-delay-c02]: **RC delay**: Wire resistance ($R$), capacitance ($C$), and loading contribute to signal propagation delay. Their values depend on geometry and materials; resistance and capacitance do not necessarily change in the same direction as a process scales. Wire delay can limit the distance that signals travel within a clock cycle.

[^fn-metastability-c02]: **Metastability**: A storage element can take longer than the available time to settle to a valid logic level when its sampling requirements are violated. Sampling an asynchronous signal is a common source. Synchronizer design reduces the probability that this behavior propagates into the receiving logic.
